content: Acute burn wounds represent complex and dynamic injuries that can evolve over time. Extensive burns not only cause localized tissue damage but also lead to systemic effects on the body. The treatment of partial thickness burn wounds focuses on promoting optimal healing, and a wide range of dressings is available for this purpose. Advances in technology and a deeper understanding of wound healing processes have driven the development of innovative dressing materials. When selecting a dressing, it is essential to consider its impact on wound healing, as well as factors such as ease of application and removal, frequency of dressing changes, cost, and patient comfort. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various burn wound dressings on the healing of superficial and partial thickness burns. For this updated review, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL, with the most recent searches performed in November 2012. The review included all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the impact of burn wound dressings on the healing process of these types of burns. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors using standardized forms, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. A total of 30 RCTs were included in this review. However, the overall quality of trial reporting and conduct was generally poor, which limited the ability to perform meta-analyses due to heterogeneity among studies and inadequate data reporting. Despite the limitations in evidence quality, certain trends were observed. Silver sulphadiazine (SSD) was consistently associated with poorer healing outcomes compared to biosynthetic dressings (skin substitutes), silver-containing dressings, and silicon-coated dressings. Additionally, burns treated with hydrogel dressings demonstrated faster healing compared to those managed with usual care. The authors concluded that there is a lack of high-quality evidence regarding the effectiveness of different dressings for superficial and partial thickness burn injuries. The studies included in this review examined a wide range of interventions, comparators, and clinical outcomes, and all were at risk of bias. As a result, it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy of specific dressings. However, the evidence suggests that silver sulphadiazine is associated with inferior healing outcomes compared to biosynthetic, silicon-coated, and silver dressings, while hydrogel dressings appear to promote better healing outcomes than standard care.
